places.name: Drake Bay

visits.text: Drake Bay (Bahía Drake) can be reached by boat from Sierpe (~1 hour), by air from San José or by road. If you take the boat, leave the car in a guarded car park in Sierpe. Drake Bay village is a base for exploring the Osa Peninsula, one of the most biodiverse areas on the planet. Plan for at least 2 nights.

Corcovado National Park, described by National Geographic as the most biologically intense place on Earth, spans 41,788 hectares of primary rainforest. It contains 2.5% of the world's biodiversity on 0.001% of Earth's surface. Jaguars, Baird's tapirs, pumas, scarlet macaws, and four monkey species coexist in this lowland forest.

Isla del Caño, a biological reserve 20 km offshore from Drake Bay, is one of Costa Rica's premier diving and snorkeling sites. Whitetip reef sharks, sea turtles, manta rays, dolphins. The pre-Columbian stone spheres scattered across the island remain an archaeological enigma.

activities.text: First evening in Drake Bay. Sunset walk along the main beach. Lodges offer guided tours for the following day—Corcovado or Isla del Caño, book upon arrival.

Corcovado or Isla del Caño—both are mutually exclusive for one day. Corcovado for hiking enthusiasts and terrestrial wildlife (jaguars, tapirs, scarlet macaws). Isla del Caño for divers and marine life lovers.

places.name: La Fortuna

visits.text: The San José–La Fortuna road crosses the Central Valley. The perfect cone of Arenal Volcano comes into view as you approach: 1,670 meters of gray basalt towering over the plain.
Downtown La Fortuna is compact: a white church, a park and a row of tour agencies. It's the ideal logistical base for three days in the region.

The Arenal 1968 trail is named after the eruption that buried three villages under lava in July of that year. Plan a round-trip drive from La Fortuna to reach its entrance. Choose between two routes: Sendero Bosque (4.7 km through the forest) or Sendero Colada (4 km, directly to the lava fields). The black, fractured terrain contrasts with the vegetation reclaiming the land.

Mirador El Silencio offers one of the most direct views of Arenal's cone. Its entrance is separate from that of the Arenal 1968 trail; plan a round-trip drive from La Fortuna. On clear days, you can also see Lake Arenal below.

Mistico Hanging Bridges park requires a round-trip drive from La Fortuna. It offers 3 km of trails with 16 bridges, including 6 suspended above the canopy. Guides equipped with spotting scopes locate sloths, toucans and howler monkeys in the trees.

La Fortuna Waterfall plunges 70 meters into an emerald pool. From the paid entrance, you need to descend about 500 steps to reach it, then climb back up on the return—the effort is considerable in intense heat.

Cerro Chato is the extinct volcano next to Arenal, but access to its crater is prohibited. From La Fortuna, plan a round-trip drive to Arenal Observatory Lodge. Walk the trails of its forest reserve to watch birds and admire Cerro Chato and Arenal from the property, without taking the closed crater trail.

activities.text: First evening in La Fortuna: a stroll around the central park and dinner at one of the local restaurants with a view of the volcano.
Settle in early—tomorrow begins with the Arenal 1968 hike at dawn, before the clouds hide the summit.

Late in the day, head to the natural hot springs near the volcano. The water, heated by geothermal activity, ranges between 25 and 38°C. A free thermal river lies near Tabacon Hot Springs, accessible by following the side of the road.
The Bogarin Trail is a private path on the edge of La Fortuna, known for sightings of two- and three-toed sloths. Local guides equipped with telescopes point out animals camouflaged in the branches.

Lake Arenal, created in 1972, is the largest in Costa Rica. Plan a round-trip drive from La Fortuna to reach the departure points for activities on the lake. Its northern shore offers views of the volcano from the water. Local operators offer kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding and boat trips.

places.name: Manuel Antonio

visits.text: The descent from Monteverde toward the central Pacific crosses the Guanacaste agricultural plain before reaching the coast. Heat replaces the humidity of the cloud forest. Quepos, a small port town 5 km from the park, serves as the area's base.

Manuel Antonio National Park (683 hectares of land) is one of Costa Rica's richest. The main trail, flat and well maintained, follows the 18-hectare mangrove before reaching Playa Manuel Antonio, considered one of the country's most beautiful beaches.

Punta Catedral is a former island connected to the mainland by a sandy tombolo, forming a whale-tail-shaped peninsula. The trail around it is temporarily closed. From Playa Manuel Antonio, observe the peninsula and the forest covering its hills, then walk along the beach without taking the closed trail.
The park's mangrove, visible from trails paralleling the beaches, covers 18 hectares of fresh and saltwater. Red and white mangroves form their own ecosystem, distinct from the adjacent rainforest.

Biesanz Bay, a few minutes' walk from the hillside hotels, is a small cove protected from the surf. The water is clear, the bottom sandy—ideal for snorkeling. Rays, parrotfish, and sometimes sea turtles make appearances.
Playa Gemelas, a small cove inside the park, is Manuel Antonio's least-visited beach. Ideal for a quiet morning between the forest and the Pacific after long days of hiking.

activities.text: In the evening, head to Playa Espadilla Norte, the public beach outside the park. This is the classic spot to watch the sunset over the Pacific. Palm trees, gentle waves, low-angle light—the postcard image of Costa Rica.
Quepos comes alive in the evening. The town is known for its fresh fish restaurants and relaxed atmosphere. A stroll along the waterfront before dinner.

Hire a certified naturalist guide at the park entrance. Equipped with a spotting scope, they'll spot two-toed sloths clinging to branches, white-headed capuchin monkeys and squirrel monkeys, endemic to Manuel Antonio. The difference between a solo visit and a guided one is considerable.
After the hike, a swim at Playa Manuel Antonio. The turquoise waters are sheltered by the forest above. Snorkeling is possible at the sides of the beach to observe moray eels, angelfish and starfish.

The kayaking excursion through the Isla Damas mangrove takes you down the Río Damas estuary over half a day. The network of channels shelters crocodiles, monkeys, shorebirds and terns. Local outfitters provide equipment and guides.
Free afternoon at the beach. Quepos has an active marina: deep-sea sportfishing trips and coastal tours depart from there, and sea kayaks are available to rent.

Board a catamaran for a cruise along the Pacific coast. The route follows the national park islands, with a snorkeling stop in waters rich with marine life. Coastal dolphins regularly accompany the boats; in season (July–November), humpback whales pass through the area.
Final evening in Quepos: dinner by the sea with fish of the day. The town is lively in the evening, with several restaurants along the waterfront.

visits.text: The La Fortuna–Monteverde road follows Lake Arenal's northern shore. It's one of the country's most scenic drives: the volcano in your rearview mirror, the winds of Tilarán as you approach, the road climbing gradually toward the cloud forest.

Santa Elena is the village that serves as a base for Monteverde. A few shopping streets are home to restaurants, tour agencies and accommodations. The atmosphere is more relaxed than in La Fortuna—it's a small mountain town at an elevation of 1,400 meters.

Santa Elena Reserve, less visited than neighboring Monteverde, covers 310 hectares at an elevation of 1,600 meters. On clear days, its lookout offers a view of Arenal Volcano and, depending on conditions, as far as both coasts.

Monteverde Biological Reserve covers more than 10,500 hectares of cloud forest at an elevation of 1,400 meters. Century-old trees disappear into the mist, and orchids—more than 500 species—grow on their trunks. Nine marked trails cross this unique ecosystem, including Sendero Bosque Nuboso, ideal for spotting the resplendent quetzal.

Curi-Cancha Reserve, 3 km from Santa Elena, draws smaller crowds than Monteverde and rivals it for biodiversity. Seven marked trails wind through 76 hectares of primary forest. Spider monkeys, capuchins, coatis, and quetzals appear regularly.

Monteverde Butterfly Garden showcases around 490 species in a screened enclosure. Butterflies emerging from their chrysalises are particularly spectacular. Children and adults alike enjoy the life-cycle demonstrations.

activities.text: Evening in Santa Elena: wander the village, sample the local cheese—a specialty of the Quaker families who settled here in the 1950s. Artisan dairies sell directly to the public.

Monteverde's canopy tour ranks among Costa Rica's most celebrated. Ziplines cross the canopy for several kilometers; some cables stretch beyond 700 meters. The circuit also includes suspension bridges and, for the bold, a Tarzan swing.

places.name: Puerto Viejo

visits.text: The return from Tortuguero involves a boat ride back to La Pavona, then a drive toward the Caribbean coast past Limón. Puerto Viejo de Talamanca is about 5-6 hours total travel time. The road hugs the coast after Limón—your first glimpse of Costa Rica's Atlantic side, very different from the Pacific: greener water, jungle straight down to the sand.

Puerto Viejo is a former fishing village that's become the epicenter of the southern Caribbean coast. Its Afro-Caribbean, Bribri, and Tico blend creates an atmosphere you won't find anywhere else in Costa Rica—reggae music, vivid colors, rondón (Caribbean coconut milk soup) served in roadside shacks.

Cahuita National Park, 20 km from Puerto Viejo, protects a coral reef in Costa Rica. The reef surrounds Punta Cahuita: 35 coral species, some reaching 2 metres in diameter, 123 fish species, nurse sharks and manta rays. In 1991, an earthquake raised the coast by a metre, damaging some of the coral - but the reef is recovering.

The park's coastal trail (8 km from Kelly Creek to Puerto Vargas) follows the beach, alternating between humid tropical forest and oceanfront. Sloths, howler monkeys, raccoons, iguanas, and countless bird species are regularly spotted. The park is community-managed and operates on a voluntary donation basis—entry is free.

The road south of Puerto Viejo passes a succession of beaches for 13 km to Manzanillo. Punta Uva is the most stunning in the area: turquoise water, golden sand, jungle right down to the shore. Playa Manzanillo, within the Refugio Nacional Gandoca-Manzanillo, marks the southern boundary of the protected zone.

The Gandoca-Manzanillo Refuge protects 10 km of beach, 740 hectares of forest, a coral reef, and two marshes. It's also a nesting area for sea turtles, manatees, crocodiles, and dolphins. Marked trails run through the forest from Manzanillo village.

activities.text: First evening in Puerto Viejo: explore the waterfront on foot or by bike. Bike rental is the local mode of transport—distances between beaches are short and the road is flat.
Snorkeling trip with a certified guide on the Cahuita reef, accessible only by boat with an escort. Local guides offer 2-hour sessions from the beach with all equipment provided.
Return to Puerto Viejo for a free afternoon at Playa Cocles, the area's most popular surf beach. Waves suitable for all levels—locals offer year-round lessons.
Full-day bike ride along the Puerto Viejo-Manzanillo coastal road. The 13 km stretch is flat, shaded, and punctuated with beaches. It's the best way to explore the coast at the local pace.
Snorkeling at Punta Uva or Manzanillo. These are the two best snorkeling spots on the Caribbean coast after Cahuita: coral reefs, tropical fish, rays, and sometimes sea turtles.

places.name: San Jose

visits.text: The National Theater of San José, inaugurated in 1897, was financed by a coffee tax imposed on Central Valley growers. Its neoclassical facade opens onto an Italian-style auditorium adorned with imported marble and paintings commissioned from European artists. It can be visited during the day, or you can attend a performance in the evening.

Beneath the Plaza de la Cultura, the Pre-Columbian Gold Museum holds more than 1,600 pieces—animal figurines, ritual jewelry, frog-shaped pendants—created by the peoples who lived in Costa Rica before the Spanish arrived. The museum's underground architecture is itself unusual.

The Jade Museum, facing Plaza de la Democracia, houses the Americas' largest collection of pre-Columbian jade. Jadeite pendants, masks, and figurines date from 500 BC to AD 800. The five-story contemporary building also includes ceramics and stone objects in their ritual contexts.

The Mercado Central, steps from the National Theater, has been the city's covered market since 1880. Tropical fruit, herbs, pottery and the day's casado are sold alongside roasted coffee. The atmosphere is that of an ordinary Costa Rican market, far removed from tourism.

Barrio Amón, north of downtown, is lined with Victorian and Art Deco houses from the early 20th century. A few galleries and cafés occupy the old homes of coffee-growing families. A good place for an end-of-trip stroll.

activities.text: Wander along Avenida Central, the pedestrian street connecting Plaza de la Cultura to Parque Central. Colorful buildings, live music and sugarcane juice vendors set the scene for a final Costa Rican afternoon.
Parque Central is downtown San José's green lung. Families of green parrots nest in the trees and appear every day in the late afternoon—a typically Costa Rican urban quirk.

visits.text: The San José–Tortuguero journey happens in two stages: road to La Pavona dock (~3 hours), then boat along the Río La Suerte and Tortuguero River canals (~1.5 hours). The two boat rides through the jungle are visits in themselves: howler monkeys in the trees, herons on the banks, vegetation closing overhead.

Tortuguero is a village of roughly 1,800 people squeezed onto a sliver of land between the Caribbean Sea and the park's canals. No cars: you get around on foot, by bike, or by boat. The main street gathers a few restaurants, souvenir shops, and tour operators.

Tortuguero National Park covers 76,937 hectares, over 50,000 at sea. Its canal network snakes through a rainforest nicknamed Costa Rica's little Amazon. The water trails—Caño Chiquero (2.3 km), Caño Harold, Caño Palma (5.1 km)—are navigable by canoe or kayak without motors to preserve silence.
The El Jaguar land trail (2.5 km, parallel to the beach) threads through the rainforest from the village. Waterproof boots are available for rent at the entrance—essential in wet conditions.

Cerro Tortuguero is a small 120-meter hill accessible by boat then on foot from the village. Its summit offers the region's only panoramic view: Caribbean Sea, canal network, and forest stretching to the horizon.

activities.text: Arrival in mid-afternoon. First evening in the village: a stroll along the main path, dinner in one of the small Caribbean restaurants with rice & beans and fresh fish. The village's only ATM often runs out of money - bring cash before you leave.

Set out on an early-morning canoe or kayak excursion through the canals, preferably without a motor. The boat glides silently under the canopy: caimans on the banks, spider and howler monkeys in the trees, green and blue kingfishers in ambush. Mornings are when wildlife is most active.

During nesting season (July–October), a guided nighttime outing on the beach lets you observe green turtles laying their eggs on the black sand. An accredited guide is mandatory. No lights or flash allowed.

places.name: Uvita

visits.text: Marino Ballena National Park, Costa Rica's first marine park (1989), is famous for its Punta Uvita tombolo: at low tide, a tongue of sand emerges from the water taking the shape—from above—of a whale's tail. Walking this sandbar with ocean on both sides is one of the country's most striking experiences.

Nauyaca Waterfalls, accessible from Dominical (~30 min north of Uvita), rank among Costa Rica's most spectacular cascades. The hike (~16 km round-trip) can also be done on horseback. Swimming permitted in the lower pool.

Returning from Drake Bay reverses the boat journey to Sierpe in the morning, then drives north along the southern Pacific coast. Dominical, a surf village 30 min from Uvita, marks the gateway to the Costa Ballena. Playa Ventanas in Ojochal—a beach framed by cliffs pierced with natural arches—is among the region's most photogenic.

Free day in Uvita and the surrounding area. In Marino Ballena National Park, walk along Uvita beach and reach the Punta Uvita tombolo at low tide. The walk follows the Pacific and lets you discover the sandbar that forms the whale's tail.

activities.text: Boat excursion for humpback whale watching (two seasons: December-April and July-October). Spotted dolphins and manta rays present year-round.

Transition and relaxation day along the coast. Beach at Dominical (surfing) or Playa Hermosa (calm swimming), lunch at one of Ojochal's small restaurants renowned for international cuisine, return to Uvita for the night.
Return to Marino Ballena National Park in the late afternoon, during admission hours, for sunset over the whale's tail. Sweeping views of the Pacific.
Snorkel around the tombolo at low tide or take a kayak trip through the mangroves of the río Sierpe, as you prefer; for the río Sierpe, allow for a round trip from Uvita during the day.
